passage:
The mill truck did not come on the Thursday before the harvest fair, and by noon my grandfather knew why: the bridge at Lenz was shut. Forty fair loaves were promised for Saturday, and the bin behind the ovens held flour for the morning rolls and little more. He did not close the shop. He did not cut the order, though the committee would have taken twenty. The rye in the cellar had sat two winters and smelled of damp, and none of it went near the trough. I bicycled to the supermarket and came back with six bags of white flour; he baked no loaf from it, would not let me return it, and none went to the neighbours or into the bin. It went to dust the boards. At four o'clock he took off his apron, crossed the square to the Varga bakery, where he had not set foot in eleven years, and asked whether Ilona Varga could spare four sacks.

She carried them out herself. It was not a sale; she pushed his money back across the counter. It was not a loan, for she wanted nothing returned. It was no peace offering, since she would still not speak of the eleven years, and she wanted no credit, not even her name on the fair table. My grandmother, she said, had lent her yeast in a bad week long ago, and that was a debt she had meant to pay.

Walking home, he told me what had decided it. It was not the money, though the fair loaves carried the shop through January. It was not the committee, which would have taken twenty and said nothing, nor the town, since nobody blames a baker for a bridge. It was not pride; he had left that on her step. "I said forty," he told me. "Forty is what I said."

We baked until two, and forty loaves went to the fair whole. I was not embarrassed that he had gone asking across the square, and the bread had never worried me. Nothing in it struck me as funny, and I felt no relief, since the eleven years were not over. I was proud of him, and ashamed that I had been sure he would never ask.
